title: Rich in Cattle, Rich in Truth
hookLine: a cowshed at dawn, jasmine on the door, eight Lakshmis, and a hymn that counts truth of speech as riches
tomorrow: why does Lakshmi always sit on a lotus?

cards: A village before sunrise smells like several things at once. Woodsmoke. Wet earth.
Milk warming in a pot. The cowshed, which nobody would call perfume. And then, from somewhere, a string of jasmine on a doorframe.
Every one of those smells means the household is alive: fuel, food, animals fed, someone who cared enough to hang flowers. Today's lines of the Sri Sukta smell like that morning.
The riches they name start in the cowshed and end in a person's mouth.

teach.b: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Her doorway is fragrance.

teach.h: RICH IN COW DUNG, QUEEN OF ALL.
teach.b: She is hard to overcome, always flourishing, rich in cow dung, the queen of all beings: I call Sri near. Yes, rich in cow dung.

It's there in the Sanskrit, karishini, right next to queen of all beings, and the hymn sees no contradiction. In a farming household, dung is fuel for the fire, food for the fields and plaster for the floor.
It means the cattle are healthy and the soil will feed you. So the goddess of fortune smells of jasmine at the door and of the cowshed out back, and both are signs of her. Now the next line.

teach.h: THE WISH, THE INTENTION, THE TRUTH.
teach.b: In paraphrase: may we gain the wish of the mind, the intention of the heart, the truth of speech. The beauty of cattle, and of food. May Sri and good name rest in me.
First it asks for things nobody can store in a barn: an intention carried through, truth in what you say. In a hymn about fortune, truth of speech is counted as riches.
And this is what Hindus mean when they say Lakshmi is more than money.
A popular later hymn praises eight Lakshmis, the Ashta Lakshmi: wealth, yes, but also grain, courage, children, knowledge and victory among them.

teach.h: TRUTH OF SPEECH, COUNTED AS RICHES.
teach.b: In village homes, cows are honored at Diwali, and floors are freshly plastered before the puja. The fortune this hymn wants is wider than a bank balance, and earthier, and it includes the way a person talks.

how: In some Hindu homes, especially in villages, cattle are honored at festivals and floors and courtyards are freshly plastered and decorated before Lakshmi worship; the Sri Sukta is chanted as part of that worship.

o: a hymn counting cattle, food and true words as riches
a farmer's song for the start of the rainy season
a hymn saying that only gold counts as wealth

games.q: what counts as riches — tap the pairs.
p: the same line as the cow dung
asked for before cattle and food

s: the hymn calls the goddess rich in cow dung
karishini, right beside queen of all beings.
the riches in these lines are only gold and cattle
they include the mind's wish, the heart's intention and truth of speech.
the hymn asks that Sri rest in the barn but not the person
it asks, may Sri and good name rest in me.

games.q: you're listing the riches you'd like the goddess to bring. after the mind's wish and the heart's intention, what comes next?
games.why: the hymn asks for truth of speech, and only then for the beauty of cattle and food. honest words are counted among the riches.

practice: Count your riches the way the eight Lakshmis do, one per breath: food today, a roof, someone who's family to you, a bit of courage, something you know, a small win.
Then turn inward: an intention you've been carrying, something true you said this week, and let that count too.
If you pray, you can give thanks to the goddess, or to God, for each; if you don't, let yourself be a little richer than you thought.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. A hymn that calls Sri fragrant at the door and rich in cow dung, and asks for truth of speech in the same breath as cattle and food.

orig.note: Sanskrit: karīṣiṇīm, 'rich in cow dung,' a name for Sri in the Sri Sukta, beside 'queen of all beings'.

carryVoice: Your line: Lakshmi is more than money. Jasmine at the door, the cowshed out back, and an honest word. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 9–10 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)
